title: Consistent hashing
scopeHtml: Scope: hash mod N problem, ring, virtual nodes, worked example, alternatives, hot keys.

notes.title: The problem with hash mod N
notes.html:
To spread keys over N servers, the simplest rule is server = hash(key) mod N. It works until N changes. Add or remove one server and almost every key maps somewhere new, so a cache loses nearly all its data at once.

Worked example. Keys 0 to 11 on 3 servers (key mod 3): server 0 holds 0,3,6,9; server 1 holds 1,4,7,10; server 2 holds 2,5,8,11. Add a 4th server (key mod 4): key 4 -> 0, key 5 -> 1, key 6 -> 2, key 7 -> 3 and so on. Counting: keys that stay put are those where k mod 3 = k mod 4: only 0, 1, 2, and 12-ish repeats, so about 3 of 12 stay (25%) and 75% move. In general, going N to N+1 moves about N/(N+1) of keys.

Production symptom. After adding one cache node, hit ratio falls from 95% to about 20%, the database gets a cache-miss storm (thundering herd), latency spikes. Metric: cache hit ratio and DB QPS jump together.

Industry examples. This is why memcached clients (libketama) and Dynamo-style stores use consistent hashing, not mod N.

Everyday analogy. Seating by "guest number mod tables": adding one table reshuffles nearly everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing mod N for a cache cluster that must scale.
  • Saying "just rehash" without cost (a cache-miss avalanche).

notes.title: The consistent hashing ring
notes.html:
Consistent hashing maps both servers and keys onto the same circle (hash ring); each key belongs to the next server clockwise. Adding or removing a server only moves the keys in one arc, about 1/N of the total on average.

Steps:

  1. Choose a hash with a big range (for example 0 to 2^32 - 1 or 2^64 - 1).
  2. Hash each server's name or IP to a point on the ring.
  3. Hash a key; move clockwise to the first server point at or after it.
  4. Replicas: also store on the next R-1 distinct servers clockwise.

Worked ring example. Ring 0 to 99 for simplicity. Servers: A at 10, B at 40, C at 70.

Ring (clockwise):  A@10 ... B@40 ... C@70 ... back to A@10

Key hash   Owner
 5         A  (next clockwise point >=5 is 10)
 25        B  (next is 40)
 55        C  (next is 70)
 85        A  (wraps around past 99 to 10)
 40        B  (equal position)

Ownership ranges:  A: (70,100)+[0,10]  = 40 slots
                   B: (10,40]          = 30 slots
                   C: (40,70]          = 30 slots

Now add D at 55. Only keys in (40,55] move from C to D (15 slots, 15% of the ring). Keys owned by A and B do not move at all. Compare mod N, where about 75% of keys moved.

Remove B: keys in (10,40] move to C (next clockwise), nothing else changes.

Industry examples. Amazon Dynamo, Apache Cassandra (token ring), Riak, Akamai (original paper by Karger et al., 1997), and memcached client libraries.

Everyday analogy. Houses on a circular street; each postman covers from the previous postman's house up to his own. A new postman only takes over part of one neighbour's route.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying keys are placed "on the nearest server" with no direction; the convention is the next clockwise point.
  • Forgetting the wrap-around from the end of the ring to the start.
  • Using a poor hash; use a uniform one (MurmurHash3, xxHash, MD5 for placement, not security).

notes.title: The imbalance problem and virtual nodes
notes.html:
With few servers, random points make uneven arcs: one server may own 50% of the ring and another 10%. Also when a server dies, ALL its load falls on its single clockwise neighbour, which may then overload and die (cascade).

Virtual nodes (vnodes): each physical server owns many points (for example 100 to 256) on the ring. Arcs average out, and a failed server's load spreads over many neighbours.

Worked example. 3 servers, 1 point each, positions 10, 40, 70 on a 0-99 ring: loads 40%, 30%, 30%. Now give each 3 vnodes with hashed positions:

A: 5, 38, 82     B: 20, 61, 90     C: 12, 47, 73
Sorted ring: 5A 12C 20B 38A 47C 61B 73C 82A 90B
Arcs ending at each point (previous point to this one):
 5A: (90,100)+[0,5] = 15   12C: 7    20B: 8    38A: 18
 47C: 9   61B: 14   73C: 12   82A: 9   90B: 8
Totals: A = 15+18+9 = 42,  B = 8+14+8 = 30,  C = 7+9+12 = 28

Still not perfectly even with 3 vnodes; with 150 vnodes each, standard deviation of load drops to a few percent (rule of thumb: error roughly 1/sqrt(vnodes)). If A dies, its 9 arcs go to different successors (C, B, ...) rather than to one node.

Weighted capacity. Give a bigger machine more vnodes (a 64 GB node gets 2x the vnodes of a 32 GB node).

Decision gravity. The vnode count is hard to change once data is placed on it, because it determines token ranges and streaming; Cassandra moved its default num_tokens from 256 to 16 (version 4.0, with a better allocation algorithm; confirm in docs) after seeing repair and streaming costs with many vnodes. More vnodes: better balance but slower repair and more metadata. Fewer: simpler but uneven.

Industry examples. Cassandra num_tokens, Riak ring with 64 partitions, Dynamo's strategy variants.

Everyday analogy. Instead of one big plot per farmer, each farmer owns many small plots scattered around; a farmer leaving spreads plots among many.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting vnodes, then being asked about the hot neighbour on failure.
  • Believing vnodes fix hot KEYS; they fix unequal key RANGES only. A single hot key still lands on one server.

notes.title: Lookup and implementation
notes.html:
Keep the ring as a sorted array (or balanced tree) of (position, node); lookup is binary search, O(log V) for V total points. Add/remove is O(V) for an array or O(log V) for a tree plus the data movement.

import bisect, hashlib

def h(s: str) -> int:
    return int(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % (2**32)

class Ring:
    def __init__(self, nodes, vnodes=100):
        self.ring = sorted((h(f"{n}#{i}"), n) for n in nodes for i in range(vnodes))
        self.points = [p for p, _ in self.ring]

    def owner(self, key: str) -> str:
        i = bisect.bisect_left(self.points, h(key)) % len(self.points)  # wrap around
        return self.ring[i][1]

r = Ring(["A", "B", "C"])
print(r.owner("user:42"))

Worked example. 100 servers x 200 vnodes = 20,000 points. Binary search takes about 15 comparisons. Memory is trivial (20,000 x 16 B = 320 KB), so every client can hold the ring and route directly.

Alternatives.

  • Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing: score = hash(key, node) for each node, pick the highest. No ring, minimal movement, O(N) per lookup; simple and good for small N (CDNs, load balancers).
  • Jump consistent hash (Google): O(log N) time, no memory, even distribution, but nodes can only be added/removed at the end (numbered buckets); good for sharding by bucket number.
  • Maglev hashing (Google): a lookup table giving near-perfect balance with minimal disruption, used in L4 load balancers.
  • Fixed slots: Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots (CRC16(key) mod 16384) assigned to nodes; moving a slot moves data explicitly. Easy to reason about, not a ring.

Decision gravity. Choosing the key-to-node scheme is a near one-way door for stored data; a client-side ring requires every client to agree on membership (gossip or config). Fixed slots/logical shards (for example 1,024 logical shards on 8 machines) make later rebalancing far easier than raw hash mod machines.

Industry examples. Redis Cluster (slots), Cassandra/Dynamo (ring), Vitess and Instagram (logical shards), Envoy/Maglev (load balancing), Discord uses consistent hashing for routing guilds to servers.

Everyday analogy. A phone book split into volumes; you look up the right volume first, then the name.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing that every client needs the same view of membership; stale rings cause misrouted keys.
  • Proposing consistent hashing for a database without addressing rebalancing and replication.

notes.title: Replication, data movement and hot keys
notes.html:
Replication on the ring: store each key on the next R distinct physical nodes clockwise (the preference list; skip vnodes belonging to the same physical node). With R = 3, a node failure still leaves two copies.

Adding a node: the new node takes over arcs from existing nodes; those nodes stream the affected keys. Throttle streaming (for example Cassandra stream_throughput_outbound) so production traffic does not suffer. For caches, just let the new node warm up, or pre-warm.

Hot keys. A celebrity's key is one key, so hashing cannot split it. Fixes: replicate hot keys and read from any replica, add a local in-process cache (short TTL 1 to 5 s), or split a key into key#1..key#k and read a random suffix (writes update all k).

Worked example. 1M reads/s on a single key and a Redis node handles 100K ops/s. Split into 16 copies key#0..key#15, each read goes to a random copy: ~62K ops/s each on 16 nodes (or 16 slots). Write cost rises 16x, acceptable for rarely-updated data.

Industry examples. Twitter and Facebook cache hot items with local caches and key replication. Cassandra's hinted handoff and anti-entropy repair handle temporarily missing replicas.

Decision gravity. Replication factor is changeable but expensive (copying data); R=3 across 3 AZs is the common default.

Everyday analogy. Photocopying a popular book so more people can read at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting vnodes of the same physical host as separate replicas.
  • Claiming consistent hashing solves hot keys or cascading failure alone.

notes.title: Where it is used and when not to
notes.html:
Use it when: servers join/leave frequently, data is distributed across many nodes, and moving everything on change is unacceptable: distributed caches, key-value stores, CDNs, sharded databases, sticky load balancing, partitioned stream processing.

Skip it when: the node count is fixed and small (a modulus is fine), you need range scans (hashing destroys ordering; use range partitioning with split/merge as HBase, Spanner or Bigtable do), or a directory service (lookup table) is simpler and rebalancing must be exact.

Worked example. Chat app: 5 cache nodes; add a 6th during growth. Consistent hashing remaps about 1/6 = 17% of keys, compared with ~83% under mod N. With 95% hit rate before, the miss rate afterwards is about 5% + 17% x 95% = 21% temporarily instead of 80+%, so the DB is hit by 4x instead of 16x.

Industry examples. DynamoDB and Cassandra (ring), Memcached via libketama, Akamai and Cloudflare (hashing to cache servers), Kafka uses key hash mod partitions (fixed partition count, so adding partitions changes key mapping: a known gotcha for ordering).

Everyday analogy. Choosing between assigned seats on a circular table (consistent) and rows of numbered seats (mod).

Common interview traps.

  • Suggesting consistent hashing for ordered/range queries.
  • Not mentioning Kafka's partition-count change problem when asked about key ordering.
  • Treating "consistent hashing" as free; clients need membership, vnodes, streaming and repair.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• hash mod N moves about N/(N+1) of keys when N changes; caches collapse.
  • Consistent hashing puts servers and keys on one ring; key goes to next server clockwise; only about 1/N of keys move.
  • Few points per server means imbalance and cascading failure; use vnodes (100 to 256 historically; fewer with smart allocation) and weights.
  • Lookup: sorted array + binary search; replicas = next R distinct physical nodes.
  • Alternatives: rendezvous, jump hash, Maglev, fixed slots (Redis 16,384); range partitioning for scans.
  • It does not fix hot keys; use key splitting, local caches and replication.

questions.promptHtml: Why is server = hash(key) mod N a bad way to spread keys over a cache cluster that changes size?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the motivating problem for consistent hashing. A candidate who cannot quantify the damage has memorised the answer without understanding it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Mod N ties every key's location to N itself. Go from N to N+1 and a key stays put only if k mod N equals k mod (N+1), so about N/(N+1) of all keys move. For a cache that means nearly everything misses at once, the database takes a miss storm, and latency spikes."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Keys 0..11 on 3 servers: key 4 lives on server 1. Add a 4th server and 4 mod 4 = 0, so it moves. Only keys 0, 1, 2 (and their repeats every 12) keep their server, about 25% stay and 75% move. At 10 nodes going to 11, about 91% of keys move.

N=5 -> 6:   ~83% of keys remap
Hit ratio:  95% before -> ~16% right after (only the 17% that stay can hit)
DB load:    5% of traffic before -> ~84% of traffic after = ~17x

The cost is not the remap itself (a cache can refill) but the synchronized refill: a cache-miss avalanche on the database.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Proposing mod N for a cache that must autoscale.
  • Saying "just rehash" without costing the avalanche.
  • Thinking the problem only appears when adding nodes; removing one (or a crash) has the same effect.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is mod N fine? -> A small, fixed node count, or fixed logical shards where you never change the modulus (and move whole shards instead).
  2. Which metric shows this happening? -> Cache hit ratio dropping while DB QPS jumps at the same moment.
  3. Can you keep mod N and still scale? -> Yes: hash into a large fixed number of logical shards (say 1,024) and map shards to machines with a directory. You move whole shards, not keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "keys get reshuffled". The senior gives the N/(N+1) figure, the DB-load multiple and the hit-ratio signature, then offers a ring or logical shards as the fix.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that scaled a memcached tier by one node at peak traffic watched hit ratio fall from the 90s to the teens and the DB fall over. Libketama-style clients exist because of this.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how a consistent hashing ring works and what happens to keys when a node is added.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic fluency: can you draw it and compute movement without hand-waving.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Servers and keys are hashed onto the same circle. A key belongs to the first server clockwise from its position. Adding a server only takes over the arc between it and its predecessor, so on average 1/N of keys move, and keys owned by everyone else stay put."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Ring 0..99, A@10, B@40, C@70
key 5->A, 25->B, 55->C, 85->A (wraps)
Add D@55: only (40,55] moves from C to D = 15% of the ring.
Remove B: (10,40] moves to C; A and C's old data stays.

Lookup is a binary search over the sorted points. Use a uniform hash (MurmurHash3, xxHash); it is for placement, not security. Replicas go on the next R-1 distinct servers clockwise.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Nearest server" without the clockwise convention.
  • Forgetting the wrap-around from the end of the ring to the start.
  • Using a weak hash that clusters points.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a node dies? -> Its arc goes entirely to the next clockwise node. That is why vnodes exist.
  2. How many keys move on add? -> About 1/N on average, not exactly; depends on where the new point lands.
  3. How does a client find the owner? -> It holds the sorted ring and binary searches, so the membership view must be shared by every client.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer draws the circle. The senior adds ownership ranges, replication on distinct physical nodes and the membership-agreement problem.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Dynamo-style stores and Cassandra token rings all start from this picture.

questions.contextHtml:
A product cache fleet has 6 memcached nodes. Client libraries pick hash(key) % 6. Peak is 200k reads/s, normal hit ratio 95%, the primary DB handles at most 30k QPS. To handle growth, an engineer adds a 7th node during the evening peak and bumps N to 7 in the client config. Within a minute:

cache_hit_ratio   95% -> 14%
db_qps            10k  -> 172k
db_p99_ms         12   -> 4,800
app 5xx           0.1% -> 38%

Cache node CPU and network look normal.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, what do you do right now, and how do you prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The new node is slow or misconfigured, restart it." It ignores that the new node is fine and that the 84% remap is the cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did all clients get the new N at once (yes, config push)? Is there request coalescing? Is the DB a read replica pool? These decide how fast I can recover.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load first: rate limit or serve stale at the edge, then roll N back to 6. The old 6 nodes still hold most of the old data (unless evicted), so hit ratio recovers quickly. Do not keep fighting forward with 7.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) mod N remap: matches the timing exactly; (b) new node cold: explains only its 1/7 share; (c) network issue: node metrics are normal, so unlikely.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare per-node hit ratio: all nodes drop, not just node 7. Compute: only keys where k mod 6 = k mod 7 (about 1/7 = 14%) can hit, matching 14%.
  5. Root cause: Changing N remaps about 6/7 = 86% of keys. The DB received 86% of 200k = 172k QPS, about 5.7x its capacity.
  6. Fix: Short term: roll back, add nodes off-peak with pre-warming (replay hot keys). Long term: consistent hashing with vnodes (a 7th node moves about 14% of keys), request coalescing/single-flight, and DB protection (circuit breaker, load shedding).
  7. Prevention: Runbook rule "never resize a mod-N cache at peak", alert on hit ratio derivative, load test a resize in staging.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not scale the DB up in panic as the main fix; it is a 6x gap and the problem is the key mapping.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if you cannot roll back? -> Warm the new mapping by dual-reading: try the new owner, fall back to the old, backfill.
  • Would consistent hashing remove the miss spike? -> It reduces it to about 14% plus 5% base miss, roughly 18% misses, about 3.6x DB load, which the DB can still absorb with coalescing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team added one cache node on Black Friday morning. The DB melted within 90 seconds. After the post-mortem they moved to a ring with 200 vnodes per node and a rule that resizes are scheduled and staged one node at a time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the new node or scales the DB blindly.
  • Hire: identifies mod N remap, rolls back, proposes consistent hashing.
  • Strong hire: computes 86% and 172k QPS, mentions single-flight and pre-warm, and states resize policy.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate wrote a ring for a client-side cache router. In staging, some keys throw a NullPointerException and, after scaling from 4 to 5 nodes, more keys move than expected. Code review is today.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Ring {
    private final TreeMap<Long, String> ring = new TreeMap<>();

    void add(String node, int vnodes) {
        for (int i = 0; i < vnodes; i++) ring.put(hash(node + i), node);
    }

    String owner(String key) {
        Long p = ring.floorKey(hash(key));
        return ring.get(p);
    }
}
class Ring {
    private val ring = java.util.TreeMap<Long, String>()

    fun add(node: String, vnodes: Int) {
        for (i in 0 until vnodes) ring[hash(node + i)] = node
    }

    fun owner(key: String): String? = ring[ring.floorKey(hash(key))]
}
questions.promptHtml: List the bugs and fix the code.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Spots only the NPE and adds a null check returning a default node, which silently sends all low-hash keys to one place.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is add called while requests are being served? Are node names fixed-width? Does membership change at runtime?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A, it is staging; I would block the merge.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) floorKey returns null when the key hash is below the first point: that is the NPE and it needs a wrap-around; (b) node + i collides: "n1"+"11" and "n11"+"1" both give "n111", so two nodes get the same point and one overwrites the other, skewing movement; (c) TreeMap is not thread-safe; a concurrent add during a lookup corrupts reads.
  4. How I'd verify: A unit test that routes keys with hash below the lowest point; a test that adds 4 then 5 nodes and counts moved keys (expect about 20%); a concurrent add/lookup stress test.
  5. Root cause: Missing wrap-around, ambiguous point naming, unsynchronised mutable structure. Also floorKey (counter-clockwise) is a valid convention only if used consistently on every client; clockwise (ceilingEntry) is the common one and the one the team expects.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
String owner(String key) {
    var e = ring.ceilingEntry(hash(key));
    if (e == null) e = ring.firstEntry();   // wrap around
    return e.getValue();
}
// point name: node + "#" + i, and publish an immutable ring snapshot on change
fun owner(key: String): String {
    val e = ring.ceilingEntry(hash(key)) ?: ring.firstEntry()  // wrap around
    return e.value
}
// point name: "$node#$i", and publish an immutable ring snapshot on change
  1. Prevention: Property test: every key maps to a node, adding a node moves at most about 2/N of keys, only keys moving to the new node.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not wrap the ring in a global synchronized lookup; copy-on-write snapshots keep lookups lock-free.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do clients agree on membership? -> Gossip or a config service with versioned membership; stale rings cause misroutes, which for a cache is tolerable and for a primary store is not.
  • Hash function? -> MurmurHash3 or xxHash, uniform; not security-critical.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a router with floor semantics worked in tests (random keys rarely fell below the first point). In production one key range always threw, only visible on 1 of 100 requests. The wrap-around test was added to the library template.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only adds a null check.
  • Hire: wrap-around, collision, thread safety.
  • Strong hire: also property tests, immutable snapshots and membership agreement.

questions.promptHtml: What are virtual nodes, what problems do they solve in consistent hashing, and what do they not solve?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the balance and failure-spreading story, and the common over-claim that vnodes fix hot keys.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "With one point per server, arcs are uneven and a dead server dumps all its load on one neighbour. Vnodes give each physical server many points, so load evens out and a failure spreads over many nodes. They fix uneven key ranges, not a single hot key."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
With 3 servers and 1 point each, one can own 50% of the ring. With V vnodes each, the relative error is roughly 1/sqrt(V). Weights: give a bigger machine more vnodes. When node A dies, each of its vnodes hands data to a different successor, so many nodes share the extra load.

1 point/server:   A dies -> neighbour gets 2x load -> may die (cascade)
150 vnodes/server: A dies -> load spreads across ~all remaining nodes

Costs: more metadata, more ranges to repair and stream (Cassandra moved the default num_tokens from 256 to 16 in 4.0 with a smarter allocator; verify the version).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming vnodes fix hot keys.
  • Not accounting for repair/streaming cost of large vnode counts.
  • Counting two vnodes on one host as separate replicas.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How many vnodes? -> Enough for balance (100 to 256 historically); fewer with a balanced allocation algorithm.
  2. Heterogeneous hardware? -> Weighted vnode counts.
  3. Why is the vnode count a near one-way door? -> It determines token ranges and streaming granularity; changing it means moving data.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "more points, better balance". The senior quantifies (1/sqrt(V)), explains failure spreading and names the repair cost trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Cassandra cluster with 256 vnodes saw slow repairs; teams lowered tokens on new clusters with the better allocator.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing a 20-node key-value tier. Nodes are identical. The SRE target: no node more than 15% above average load in steady state. A colleague proposes 8 vnodes per node "to keep metadata small"; another proposes 1,000 "for perfect balance". The store streams data per range on node add and repairs per range.
questions.promptHtml: Which vnode count do you pick, and how do you justify it with numbers?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks a number from a blog post with no balance estimate or cost discussion.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the store's allocator balance ranges (then fewer vnodes suffice)? How expensive is per-range repair? Is the workload skewed by key?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A, design question. First decision: confirm that skew comes from ranges, not hot keys, since vnodes do not fix hot keys.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Relative std dev about 1/sqrt(V). V=8: about 35%, far above target. V=100: 10%. V=200: about 7%. V=1,000: about 3%.
  4. How I'd verify: Simulate: hash 20 nodes x V points, hash 1M keys, measure max/avg for V in {8, 64, 128, 256, 1000}; repeat 100 random seeds and take the p99 of max/avg.
  5. Root cause of the trade-off: The tail is max over 20 nodes, roughly avg + 2 sigma, so I need sigma at about 7% or lower, giving V about 200.
  6. Fix: Choose about 128 to 256 (if no smart allocator); 20 x 200 = 4,000 points is tiny for the client ring. If the store has a balanced allocator, 16 to 32 can reach the target; verify in the docs for the version.
  7. Prevention: Track per-node data size and QPS as a balance dashboard; alert when max/avg exceeds 1.15.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not pick 1,000: repair and streaming overhead grows with range count, and the marginal balance gain is small. I would not pick 8: the target is missed by a wide margin.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mixed 32 GB and 64 GB nodes? -> Weight: 2x vnodes for the bigger one.
  • One node still hot? -> Check for a hot key; vnodes will not fix it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team shipped 16 random tokens per node on an old version without an allocator and had a 2x spread between the busiest and idlest node for months.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: guesses.
  • Hire: uses 1/sqrt(V) and picks about 100-256.
  • Strong hire: simulates, discusses allocator, repair cost and hot keys separately.

questions.contextHtml:
A 4-node cache tier uses a consistent hash ring with 1 point per node. All nodes run at 65% CPU at peak. Node B crashes (OOM). Over the next 4 minutes:

t+0:00  B down.        C cpu 65% -> 98%
t+1:30  C p99 800 ms, timeouts, C OOM-killed
t+2:00  D cpu 62% -> 96% (took C's arcs)
t+3:30  D down. Only A left, DB at 100%.

Restart of B and C later makes things worse: they come up empty.
questions.promptHtml: Why did a single failure cascade, and how do you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more nodes" with no explanation of why the failure moved to the successor.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there replication? Is there request coalescing and DB protection? Is autoscaling in play?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load (cap QPS, serve degraded), stop clients retrying, bring restarted nodes in one at a time with warming, and keep the DB protected with a circuit breaker.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) successor takes the whole dead arc: B's load all lands on C (65% + 65% = 130% demand); (b) restarts cause a cold-cache wave; (c) retry amplification.
  4. How I'd verify: Ring ownership map shows B's arc is adjacent to C's only; per-node QPS jumped by about B's share onto C only; client retry metrics.
  5. Root cause: One point per node means a failed node's load goes to exactly one neighbour, and the system had no headroom: with N=4, tolerating one failure requires steady utilisation at or below (N-1)/N = 75%, and a single neighbour needs even more.
  6. Fix: 100+ vnodes per node so B's load spreads: each of 3 survivors takes about 22%, utilisation 65% -> about 87%, which is survivable. Add headroom (target 60% peak), load shedding and request coalescing; stagger restarts.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test: kill one node at peak monthly; alert on per-node utilisation skew; capacity rule N-1 at p99 peak.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not simply add a 5th node on the same ring layout (the neighbour problem remains) and I would not turn off retries blindly; use budgets and jitter.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Replicas help? -> Yes for availability of data, but the extra read load still needs capacity.
  • What if the failure is a deploy, not a crash? -> Drain nodes one at a time so only a small arc is cold at any moment.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a 6-node tier lost one node at lunch peak. Because each node ran at about 80%, the three adjacent nodes saturated in a chain. The fix was vnodes plus a 60% peak utilisation rule.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "more nodes".
  • Hire: neighbour takeover, vnodes, headroom.
  • Strong hire: N-1 math, retry amplification, staggered warm-up and chaos testing.

questions.contextHtml: A livestream platform caches viewer-count and stream metadata in Redis, sharded by consistent hashing over 20 nodes. A celebrity goes live: one key stream:meta:777 receives 1M reads/s. One Redis node serves about 100k ops/s and sits at 100% CPU, with p99 over 900 ms; the other 19 nodes are at 8%. Adding nodes changes nothing. The app has 400 servers. The key is updated about once every 5 seconds.
questions.promptHtml: How do you fix it, and why will the obvious fix not work?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more nodes / more vnodes." Hashing sends one key to one node regardless of the count.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How stale may the data be (seconds)? Is it read-mostly? Can the key be updated by many writers? Do we know the key set that is hot (detection)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a local in-process cache with 1 to 2 s TTL for that key on every app server; takes the load off Redis immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: One hot key (the evidence: 1 node at 100%, others 8%); not imbalance of ranges.
  4. How I'd verify: redis-cli --hotkeys (needs LFU policy) or MONITOR sampling briefly; per-key counters at the client.
  5. Root cause: Consistent hashing balances key ranges, not per-key traffic. One key lives on one node.
  6. Fix: Local cache: 400 servers x 0.5 refreshes/s = 200 reads/s to Redis, a 5,000x reduction. Alternatively replicate the key as key#0..key#15, reads pick a random copy: 1M / 16 = 62.5k ops/s each, under the 100k limit; writes go to all 16 (16x write cost, fine at 1 write per 5 s).
  7. Prevention: Hot-key detection in the client library that auto-promotes keys to local cache, plus per-key QPS dashboards.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Local cache adds staleness of up to the TTL; if the data must be exact (inventory), do not use it. I would not shard the key unless it is read-heavy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A hot key that is written 10k/s (a counter)? -> Shard writes: key#i increments, sum on read, or aggregate in memory and flush.
  • Thundering herd when the local cache expires? -> Jittered TTLs and single-flight.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a global event pushed one config key to 700k reads/s. The fix was a 1 s in-process cache with jitter; Redis load dropped by orders of magnitude within one deploy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds nodes.
  • Hire: local cache or key replication, explains why.
  • Strong hire: does the math (200 reads/s, 62.5k/s), detection tooling, write cost and staleness trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: Compare ring-based consistent hashing with rendezvous hashing, jump consistent hash, Maglev and Redis Cluster's fixed hash slots. When would you choose each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers should know that the ring is one of several schemes and choose by constraints (membership shape, lookup cost, rebalancing control).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Ring with vnodes for elastic membership and replication on preference lists. Rendezvous for small N, simple and balanced, O(N) per lookup. Jump hash when buckets are numbered and only grow at the end, zero memory. Maglev for L4 load balancers where balance and minimal disruption matter. Fixed slots like Redis Cluster's 16,384 when I want explicit, controllable data movement."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Scheme        Lookup     Memory       Add/remove node        Best for
Ring+vnodes   O(log V)   V points     any node, ~1/N moves   KV stores, caches
Rendezvous    O(N)       none         any node, ~1/N moves   small N, LBs, CDNs
Jump hash     O(log N)   none         only at the end        sharding by bucket id
Maglev        O(1) table table        minimal disruption     L4 load balancers
Fixed slots   O(1)       slot map     move slots explicitly  Redis Cluster

Rendezvous: score(key,node) = hash(key,node), highest wins. With 100 nodes, 100 hashes per lookup, still microseconds. Jump hash cannot remove an arbitrary node (only the last bucket), so it needs a mapping layer for failures.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using jump hash where a middle node can fail.
  • Using rendezvous with 10,000 nodes on a hot path.
  • Treating "consistent hashing" as free: clients need a shared membership view.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Redis Cluster not use a ring? -> Fixed 16,384 slots give explicit, resumable migration and simple routing by CRC16 mod 16384.
  2. How do you replicate with rendezvous? -> Take the top R scores.
  3. How do logical shards help any scheme? -> 1,024 logical shards on 8 machines means rebalancing moves whole shards, not raw keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows only the ring. The senior chooses per constraint and brings up the lookup-cost and membership trade-offs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that hashed users to machines by raw mod machines could not grow; they retrofitted logical shards and a directory.

questions.contextHtml: An orders topic has 12 partitions; producers key by orderId and the default partitioner computes hash(key) mod partitions (verify for your client). Consumers rely on per-order ordering (CREATED before PAID before SHIPPED). Lag is growing at peak (350k msgs/s), and the team wants 24 partitions. The platform engineer runs kafka-topics --alter --partitions 24 on a Tuesday. By Wednesday support sees orders marked SHIPPED before PAID.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and how do you scale partitions safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames consumer bugs or clock skew. The mapping changed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the ordering per key truly required? How long does an order live (events spread over hours)? Can consumers be paused? Are there compacted topics?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Have consumers tolerate out-of-order by state-machine guards and idempotent handlers; repair affected orders from the source of truth.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) key to partition mapping changed: events for a live order now go to a different partition than earlier ones; two consumers process them concurrently; (b) consumer rebalance reorder (less likely, ordering within a partition is kept); (c) producer retries with max.in.flight > 1 without idempotence.
  4. How I'd verify: Pick an affected order, list its events with partition and offset: the early events are in partition 3, later ones in partition 17.
  5. Root cause: hash mod partition count is mod N: changing 12 to 24 moves about half the keys (a key stays only if hash mod 12 = hash mod 24, about 50%).
  6. Fix: Short term: tolerate and repair. Long term: for ordering-critical topics, create a new topic with 24 partitions, dual-write or mirror, drain the old topic fully per key, then switch consumers (cutover per key group or in a maintenance window). Better still: over-provision partitions up front (for example 48 for expected growth).
  7. Prevention: Policy: partition count is a one-way door for keyed topics; capacity-plan partitions for 2 to 3 years; a runbook forbids --alter --partitions on keyed topics.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More partitions cost broker memory, file handles and longer recovery; I would not jump to thousands "just in case".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could consistent hashing avoid this? -> Only with a custom partitioner and still would need stateful migration; Kafka assigns keys by partition id.
  • Compacted topics? -> Even worse: the same key can exist in two partitions after the change, breaking compaction semantics.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a payments team doubled partitions and saw duplicate ledger entries for in-flight transactions. They moved to a topic migration with a drained cutover and fixed the partition count at 96.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames consumers.
  • Hire: identifies mod N remap, proposes new topic.
  • Strong hire: ordering vs idempotence, dual-write cutover, up-front capacity planning, compacted-topic caveat.

questions.contextHtml: A PM says: "Our orders table (3 TB, growing 100 GB/month) is too big for one Postgres. Shard it with consistent hashing, we will add shards every quarter. Also finance runs daily reports by date range and the support tool lists a customer's orders newest first." There are 5 engineers and no existing sharding infrastructure.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond and what do you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure: put a ring in the app, hash order id, done." It ignores range queries, rebalancing and operations.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the access pattern split: point lookups by order id, by customer, by date range? Do queries cross customers (joins)? Is growth write load or storage? What RPO/latency matters? Could we archive old orders instead?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Before sharding: partition by month, archive cold data, add read replicas, check indexes; 3 TB is large but not automatically a sharding case.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The real needs: (a) customer-centric reads: shard by customer_id, keeps a customer's orders on one shard and keeps "list my orders" single-shard; (b) reports are analytic: send them to a warehouse via CDC rather than scatter-gather; (c) raw consistent hashing of order id would scatter a customer's orders.
  4. How I'd verify: Query logs by pattern, p99 and frequency; test a prototype on production-shaped data.
  5. Root cause of the confusion: Hashing destroys ordering so date-range scans fan out to every shard; and a ring is a placement scheme, not a database sharding system: it needs resharding, cross-shard transactions, id generation and routing.
  6. Fix: Hash customer_id into 1,024 logical shards, map logical shards to 8 physical Postgres instances via a directory; adding capacity moves whole logical shards. Daily reports use a warehouse. Consider an off-the-shelf layer (Citus or Vitess-style routing; verify fit).
  7. Prevention: Shard key review, runbook for shard moves, test of cross-shard queries.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a raw ring with vnodes for a relational store; and I would not shard until simpler options are exhausted since sharding is close to a one-way door.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Customer with 50% of the data (a marketplace seller)? -> Shard by order id for that tenant or split the tenant across logical shards.
  • Global unique order ids? -> Snowflake-style ids carrying the shard id.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team hashed by order id, then discovered that "my orders" scatter-gathered across 16 shards and p99 tripled. Re-keying by customer took a quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the request unchanged.
  • Hire: clarifies queries, picks customer key, notes range scan issue.
  • Strong hire: logical shards with directory, warehouse for reports, delays sharding until needed.

questions.contextHtml:
An in-house KV store replicates each key to the next 3 ring points clockwise (RF=3). The ring has 5 hosts x 128 vnodes. During a host failure test, host H3 is powered off. Reads at QUORUM (2 of 3) fail for a large share of keys:

unavailable_errors  (quorum): 0 -> 21% of requests
logs: "only 1 live replica for token range 0x4a..0x5c (replicas: H3,H3,H1)"

Writes at QUORUM also fail on those ranges. Dashboards claim "RF=3".
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: cause, impact estimate, fix and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Network issue" or "add a 6th node".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How is the preference list built (next 3 points or next 3 distinct hosts)? Rack/AZ awareness? Any data lost or only unavailable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Power H3 back on; lower read consistency to ONE for affected tables if staleness is acceptable; stop the test.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) replicas chosen by points, not distinct hosts: log shows H3 twice in one list; (b) rack placement ignored; (c) a replica was already down.
  4. How I'd verify: Dump the preference list for sample keys and count distinct hosts; compute the fraction with fewer than 3.
  5. Root cause: With 5 hosts, the chance that 3 consecutive points belong to 3 distinct hosts is roughly (4/5) x (3/5) = 48%, so about 52% of ranges had a duplicate host. Those ranges effectively had RF 2 or even 1. Losing H3 left a single replica for part of them.
  6. Fix: Walk clockwise and skip points belonging to a host already chosen (and prefer different racks/AZs). Then repair/stream data to the correct replicas.
  7. Prevention: Invariant test: for every range, replicas are distinct hosts and distinct failure domains; a dashboard of "ranges with fewer than RF distinct hosts"; run failure drills.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just bump RF to 5 to hide the bug; that spends 67% more storage and leaves the invariant broken.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is the 21% lower than 52%? -> Only ranges whose duplicate involved H3 and whose remaining replicas failed to reach quorum were affected.
  • Impact on data durability? -> Ranges with two copies on one host lose both on one disk failure.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a hand-rolled ring passed all functional tests and failed only the first host-kill drill. The "distinct hosts" invariant became a CI property test.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the network.
  • Hire: finds duplicate host in the preference list and fixes with distinct-host walk.
  • Strong hire: computes the probability, adds failure-domain awareness, invariant test and drills.
